**Sub-item 1 — Accesses all elements in historyList and mathList (no bounds errors)**

Award the point whenever the response reaches the elements by iterating the lists themselves: an enhanced for-each over `historyList` and/or `mathList`, or an indexed loop whose bound is that same list's own `size()`. Such traversal inherently touches every element, so the "accesses all elements" requirement is met — including when the indexed loop's bound comes from the *other* list, and including when the element access sits inside a conditional. Specifically, if the loop iterates with correct bounds and a `get(i)` call appears anywhere in the loop body — inside an `if` block, inside a short-circuited expression such as `if (x) { ... mathList.get(j) ... }`, or otherwise guarded — the presence of that correctly-indexed access in the body satisfies the item; do not treat the guard as making access non-guaranteed. The point also survives when the loop variable is unused in the body, when the accessed value is discarded, or when the response returns early, as long as bounds and indices would otherwise support accessing all elements.

Deduct only for the explicitly listed defects: using array syntax to reach ArrayList elements (`historyList[i]`), using an index that is out of bounds, accessing only one of the two lists, or having an indexed loop with correct bounds that never accesses an element inside the loop at all. Other syntactic slips in the access expression — `historyList.length`, `historyList.size`, `get(i)` with an implicit receiver, `historyList.get[i]` — are minor notation errors and do not by themselves cost this point, provided the intent to access each element with a legal index is clear.
2:
# Grading Note — Sub-item 2: Calls getStudentID and getAbsences on an element from one of the lists

Award the point whenever the response invokes both accessors, with call syntax, on a CourseRecord element drawn from historyList or mathList — for example `hist.getStudentID()` and `math.getAbsences()` — regardless of how that element was obtained (enhanced for-loop variable, indexed `get(i)`, nested loops, or even array-style `[ ]` indexing) and regardless of whether the surrounding comparison logic is sound (`>=` instead of `>`, `==` on Strings, missing break, bounds errors all remain irrelevant here). Read the calls generously: if the intent is unmistakable and the receiver is a CourseRecord element, minor name-case or spelling slips, a stray argument, or near-miss syntax still count as calling getStudentID and getAbsences. The calls need only appear somewhere in executable source; it does not matter whether control flow ever reaches them, so a loop that cannot iterate, code following an unconditional return, or a branch that is never taken still satisfies the requirement. Scope the judgment to the best qualifying occurrence rather than the whole file: once at least one correct call to getStudentID and at least one correct call to getAbsences on a CourseRecord element exist, additional stray or malformed invocations elsewhere — in dead code, an unused helper, a commented-out attempt, or a second redundant loop — do not by themselves cost the point.

Deduct only when a method is applied to a receiver that is not a CourseRecord object (e.g., invoked on the ArrayList itself, on a String, or on an int), or when one of the two methods is never invoked anywhere at all.
3:
**Item 3 — Determines whether an element from one list has more absences than an element from the other list**

Award the point (no_deduct) if the response contains, anywhere in the method, at least one strict greater-than comparison between absence values obtained from `CourseRecord` objects — that is, a comparison of the form `a.getAbsences() > b.getAbsences()` (or equivalent). Read this requirement loosely in every direction the forks settle:

- **Direction does not matter.** A comparison that tests whether the math element has more absences than the history element earns the point just as much as the intended history-over-math test. The item only asks whether the response determines that one element has more absences than the other; a reversed direction still earns the point, and the resulting wrong count is penalized under item 5.
- **Which list the operands come from does not matter.** A strict greater-than comparison of absence values from `CourseRecord` objects counts even if both operands come from the same list, or if one operand is a local variable or accumulator holding an absence count. The comparison logic itself is what is being graded; correctness of pairing is handled by item 5.
- **One correct comparison anywhere suffices.** If at least one strict greater-than absences comparison appears, the point is earned even if the response elsewhere also compares absences using `>=`, `==`, `!=`, or in the wrong direction. Other incorrect comparisons do not forfeit the point.
- **The comparison need not control executed code.** A correctly formed strict greater-than comparison of two elements' absences earns the point even if its result is discarded (e.g., assigned to an unused boolean), the `if`-body is empty, or the code is unreachable or placed after a `return`.

Note also that an incorrect access of a `CourseRecord` object or `ArrayList`, or an incorrect call to the absences method, does not by itself cost this point.

Deduct (no point) only if the response contains no strict greater-than comparison of absence values at all — for example, if every absences comparison uses `>=`, `<=`, `==`, or `!=`, if the condition's logic is otherwise incorrect, or if the response never calls the absences method / never compares absence values.
4:
# Grading Note — Sub-item 4: Initializes count and increments it within a conditional statement (in the context of a loop)

Award the point only when the response both (a) initializes a count variable before the loop (or otherwise outside any loop that would reset it) and (b) places the increment statement physically inside the body of a conditional statement — an `if`, `else`, `else if`, or `switch` case — that itself sits within a loop. The initialization may be incorrect (e.g., wrong starting value) and the response may fail to identify all necessary students, return early, or call `getStudentID`/`getAbsences` incorrectly or not at all; none of these affect this point.

Deduct if the count is never initialized, or if it is initialized (or reset) inside a loop so that it restarts on each iteration. Deduct as well whenever the increment statement is not itself contained in the body of a conditional statement, even if the logic effectively guards it: guard-and-continue patterns (e.g., `if (...) continue;` followed by an unconditional `count++`), ternary-expression counting (e.g., `count += (cond) ? 1 : 0`), and boolean short-circuit tricks (e.g., `cond && count++ > 0`) all fail, because the increment itself is not inside a conditional statement. An unconditional `count++` in the loop body likewise earns no credit.
5:
**Item 5 — Returns count of all and only necessary students (algorithm)**

Award the point when the response returns the correct count, comparing every necessary pair of records on both student ID and absences. When judging how the response matches records across the two lists, treat a String comparison of the student IDs with `.equals()` — e.g., `hist.getStudentID().equals(math.getStudentID())` — as a valid String comparison and do **not** deduct for it; this is the correct way to match IDs and should never be counted against the response on this item. Deduct only for the substantive algorithmic failures: failing to return the computed value, returning an incorrect value because of an early return, failing to compare all necessary pairs of elements, using `==` to compare the String IDs, modifying either list, failing to compare both IDs and absences, or printing the count instead of (or in addition to) returning it. Incorrect access of a `CourseRecord` object or an `ArrayList`, loops that stop early or late due to incorrect bounds, and array syntax (`[ ]`) used on `ArrayList` elements are not grounds for deduction here.
